How to Use Bacillus Subtilis  Step by Step
Mix 2.5 to 5 grams in 1 litre of water. Spray in early morning or late evening. Cover both upper and lower side of leaves. Do not spray in hot sun. Repeat every 7 to 10 days during disease season.
Mix 5 to 10 grams per kg of seed. Add a little water to make a paste. Coat the seeds. Dry in shade. Sow within 24 hours.
Mix 2.5 kg per acre with 50 to 100 kg well-rotted FYM (gobar khaad) or vermicompost. Keep moist for 5 to 7 days. Then spread in the field at sowing or transplanting time.
Mix 5 grams in 1 litre of water. Pour around the base of plants. Repeat after 10 to 15 days if disease is still there.
Mix 10 grams in 1 litre of water. Dip seedling roots for 20 to 30 minutes. Then transplant.

Ampelomyces quisqualis is a special friendly fungus. It does only one job but it does it better than any other biological. It enters inside the powdery mildew fungus and eats it from inside. The white powder slowly disappears. Powdery mildew cannot grow new spores. Plant gets clean and healthy again.

Krishikranti Bhoogol Tricyclazole 75% WP is a powerful systemic fungicide made specially for blast disease control in paddy (rice). It stops all 3 types of blast  leaf blast, node blast, and the most dangerous neck blast. The spray gets absorbed into the plant within 1 to 2 hours and protects new growth for 10 to 14 days. Best fungicide for paddy farmers who want to save the crop from blast and protect their yield.

Blast is the most dangerous fungal disease in rice. It is caused by a fungus called Magnaporthe oryzae. It can destroy a paddy crop in 7–10 days if not stopped in time. Blast attacks paddy in 3 stages  and each stage can wipe out the yield.
Small spindle-shaped spots on leaves. Spots are grey in the centre and brown at the edges. As disease grows, full leaves dry up. This stage starts in the nursery or at tillering.
Black-brown rings come on the joints (nodes) of the paddy plant. The plant becomes weak and breaks easily. This stage usually comes after tillering.

This is the most dangerous stage. A black band forms at the neck where the panicle (ear-head) connects to the stem. The panicle dries up. Grains do not fill. Whole panicles become empty. This is the stage where farmers lose 50 to 80 percent of their yield.
Important: Once you see neck blast, it is too late. You must spray Tricyclazole before neck blast comes  at the booting stage, just before panicle emergence.

Tricyclazole works in a smart way. The blast fungus needs a hard black coating (called melanin) to enter the rice plant. Tricyclazole stops the fungus from making this melanin. Without melanin, the fungus cannot punch into the plant. It stays outside the leaf and dies.

Q. What is the dose of Tebuconazole 25.9% EC per acre? Standard dose is 250 ml per acre for most crops. For severe disease, use up to 300 ml per acre. Mix in 200 litres of water for one acre spray.
Q. How much Tebuconazole 25.9% EC to mix in 1 litre water? Mix 1 to 2 ml per litre of water. For knapsack sprayer (15-litre tank), mix 15 to 30 ml.

Q. Can Tebuconazole control sheath blight in paddy? Yes. It is one of the best fungicides for sheath blight in paddy. Spray 250 ml per acre at tillering stage. Repeat at booting before panicle emergence. Cover the lower part of plant where sheath blight starts.

Q. Can Tebuconazole control tikka disease in groundnut? Yes. Tebuconazole 25.9% EC is the most popular fungicide for tikka leaf spot in groundnut. First spray 30 to 40 days after sowing. Second spray 15 days later. Use 200 to 250 ml per acre.

Q. Can it stop powdery mildew in chilli and mango? Yes. Spray 250 to 300 ml per acre (1 to 1.5 ml per litre water) at first sign of white powder. Repeat after 12 to 15 days. Best results when sprayed in early morning or late evening.
Q. Will rain wash off Tebuconazole? No. Tebuconazole is rainfast within 1 to 2 hours. After absorption, it moves inside the plant. Even heavy rain will not wash off the protection.
Q. How long does Tebuconazole protect the crop? One spray gives 12 to 15 days of protection. The medicine stays active inside the plant and protects new growth that comes after spraying.
Q. Can Tebuconazole be mixed with insecticides? Yes. It is compatible with most insecticides used for stem borer, leaf folder, thrips, aphids, and whitefly. Always do a small test mix first.

Q. Is Tebuconazole the same as Folicur? Yes. Folicur is the original Bayer brand of Tebuconazole 25.9% EC. The active ingredient and dose are the same. Krishikranti Timon contains the same Tebuconazole 25.9% EC at a more farmer-friendly price.

Q. Is Tebuconazole safe for crops? Yes. When used at the recommended dose, Tebuconazole is safe and even gives a greening effect on leaves. Higher than recommended dose can cause leaf damage. Always follow the dose chart.

Q. What is the difference between Tebuconazole and Hexaconazole? Both are triazole fungicides used for similar diseases. Tebuconazole has wider crop coverage (paddy, chilli, groundnut, onion, soybean), better systemic action, and gives a stronger greening effect. Hexaconazole is mainly used for paddy sheath blight and powdery mildew.

Q. When should I stop spraying Tebuconazole before harvest? Stop spraying at least 30 days before harvest. This is the Pre-Harvest Interval (PHI) and ensures no chemical residue remains on the produce.

Powdery mildew is a white powder-like fungus that grows on plant leaves, stems, flowers, and fruits. It looks like the plant has been dusted with white flour or chalk. The white powder slowly turns yellow, then brown. Leaves dry up. Plants stop growing. Fruits stop developing. Yield drops badly.

It is a major problem in grapes, cucumber, pumpkin, bitter gourd, mango, apple, chilli, strawberry, pea, rose, tomato, and okra (bhendi). It spreads fastest in humid weather, cloudy days, and morning dew.

Ampelomyces quisqualis is a friendly fungus. But it does only one job — it eats powdery mildew. Nothing else. It is the world's only biological that kills powdery mildew from inside the disease itself.
This is called hyperparasitism  one fungus killing another fungus. It works on all kinds of powdery mildew (Erysiphe, Sphaerotheca, Podosphaera, Uncinula, Leveillula, Oidium).

Important  Be Honest: This product stops only powdery mildew. It does NOT control downy mildew, blight, anthracnose, leaf spot, or wilt. For those, see other bio fungicides like Pseudomonas fluorescens or Trichoderma viride.

Deltamethrin 11% EC : Fast-Acting Pyrethroid Insecticide for Crop Pest Control

Deltamethrin 11% EC is a synthetic pyrethroid insecticide in emulsifiable concentrate form. It controls sucking pests, chewing insects, and boring pests in cotton, paddy, chilli, tomato, brinjal, okra, pulses, and oilseeds. It acts through contact and stomach action, delivering fast knockdown of active pest populations within hours of spraying.

The 11% EC formulation provides higher active ingredient concentration per litre compared to standard 2.5% and 2.8% deltamethrin formulations, meaning lower product volume per acre with equivalent or stronger pest control.

Do not spray during flowering  deltamethrin is highly toxic to bees

Mode of Action : How Deltamethrin 11% EC Works

Deltamethrin is a Type II synthetic pyrethroid that acts on voltage-gated sodium channels in the insect nervous system. It binds to sodium channels and keeps them open, causing continuous nerve firing, convulsions, paralysis, and death. This mechanism produces rapid knockdown  pests stop feeding and fall within minutes to hours of contact.

Unlike systemic insecticides, deltamethrin works primarily through direct contact and ingestion. Thorough spray coverage is therefore critical for maximum efficacy. It has no systemic uptake into plant tissue  pests must contact the treated surface or ingest treated plant material to be controlled.

Do not mix with alkaline compounds. Store in cool, dry place away from food, feed, and livestock.

column1: What is the dose of Deltamethrin 11% EC per litre of water?

What is the difference between Deltamethrin 11% EC and 2.5% SC?

Deltamethrin 11% EC has a much higher active ingredient concentration  11% vs 2.5%. This means you need a significantly lower product volume per acre with the 11% EC formulation for equivalent pest control. The EC form also provides faster initial knockdown due to the oil-based carrier.

Contact knockdown starts within hours of spraying. Pests stop feeding almost immediately after contact with treated surfaces. Residual protection on the crop canopy lasts 7–10 days depending on rainfall and temperature.
Can Deltamethrin 11% EC be used for stem borer control in paddy?

Yes. Spray at 0.5 ml per litre (100–150 ml per acre) at the tillering stage when dead hearts first appear. Ensure spray reaches the base of tillers where stem borer larvae enter. Repeat after 14 days if infestation continues.
Can Deltamethrin 11% EC be used for bollworm control in cotton?

Yes. Apply at the first sign of bollworm egg laying or early instar larvae at 0.5 ml per litre. Stomach action kills larvae that feed on treated bolls and leaves. For heavy infestations, rotate with a diamide or organophosphate to prevent pyrethroid resistance.
What is the pre-harvest interval for Deltamethrin 11% EC?
Pre-harvest interval is 7 days for vegetables, 10 days for pulses, and 14 days for cotton and paddy. Do not harvest within this period after the last spray.
Which IRAC group is Deltamethrin and how to rotate?
Deltamethrin belongs to IRAC Group 3A (Pyrethroid). Rotate with Group 1A organophosphates, Group 4A neonicotinoids, or Group 28 diamides to prevent resistance buildup in pest populations.

Imidacloprid 70% WG : Systemic Insecticide for Sucking Pest Control

Imidacloprid 70% WG is a systemic neonicotinoid insecticide in water dispersible granule form. It controls whitefly, aphids, jassids, thrips, and planthoppers in cotton, paddy, chilli, tomato, okra, and sugarcane. The WG formulation dissolves completely in water, leaves no oily residue, and works through both contact and systemic action.

column3: >Water volume: 200 litres per acre. Mixing tip: Dissolve granules in a small quantity of water first, stir well, then add to full sprayer volume. Repeat: Every 14–21 days based on pest pressure.

column1: • Spray at first appearance of sucking pests : early application prevents population build-up
• Cover the underside of leaves thoroughly : whitefly, jassids, and aphids cluster there
• Spray in early morning or evening : avoid peak heat and windy conditions
• Do not spray during flowering when bees are foraging : imidacloprid is toxic to bees
Pre-harvest interval (PHI): 7 days for vegetables, 14 days for cotton and paddy

Imidacloprid binds to nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs) in the insect nervous system. This causes continuous nerve excitation, leading to paralysis and death. Because it is systemic, the molecule is absorbed through leaves and roots and moves through plant vascular tissue  reaching pests feeding on sap from inside the leaf, not just those on the surface. Residual activity lasts 10–14 days per foliar application.

column3: >Important: Toxic to bees and aquatic organisms  do not spray near water bodies or during pollination. Pre-harvest interval: 7 days for vegetables, 14 days for cotton and paddy. Wear gloves, mask, and full-sleeve clothing during application. Do not mix with alkaline compounds. Store in a cool, dry place away from food and livestock.

Yes. Imidacloprid 70% WG is effective against whitefly in cotton at 0.25–0.3 g per litre. Spray at first appearance of adults on leaf undersides. Rotate with non-neonicotinoid insecticides after 2 sprays to manage resistance.
What is the difference between Imidacloprid 70% WG and 17.8% SL?

Imidacloprid 70% WG has a higher concentration of active ingredient per kg — it requires a much lower product dose per acre (20–25 g) compared to 17.8% SL (100–200 ml). The WG form is easier to measure, store, and transport with lower packaging waste.
Contact action begins within a few hours of spraying. Systemic absorption is complete within 24–48 hours. Full residual protection lasts 10–14 days depending on pest pressure and crop canopy.
Is Imidacloprid 70% WG safe for use in paddy?
Yes. It is registered for BPH and green leafhopper control in paddy. Apply at 20–25 g per acre. Observe the 14-day pre-harvest interval before harvesting.
